title: OpenAI countersues Apple and accuses it of stealing trade secrets
text:
OpenAI countersues Apple and accuses it of stealing trade secrets
The suit suggests that the iPhone maker is trying to “compete unfairly by any means available.”
OpenAI has filed a major lawsuit against Apple that accuses the iPhone maker of stealing trade secrets, according to a report by Financial Times . The folks behind ChatGPT have also accused Apple of "coercing and threatening" suppliers who work with both companies. OpenAI says Apple is trying to "compete unfairly by any means available", which includes encouraging employees to store corporate files on personal devices and cloud storage accounts.
The complaint is filled with flowery language that suggests "Apple set quite a trap for employees" and that "bright young minds thought they would work in Cupertino. Instead they were joining Hotel California: you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave."
This follows a suit issued by Apple against OpenAI that accused the AI company of stealing secret trade information . This was filed after OpenAI acquired an entity called io , which is a studio led by Apple's former design chief Jony Ive. At that point, Apple called ChatGPT "rotten to its core." Now it looks like OpenAI is getting involved in a bit of tit for tat.
Apple has yet to comment on today's lawsuit, but it wasn't that long ago in which the two companies were partnered up to bring ChatGPT to iPhones . Now OpenAI is prepping its own line of hardware products that could directly compete with Apple.
To that end, the company has accused a former employee of returning to Apple and sharing details about product plans and suppliers . This is pretty much the exact same thing Apple accused OpenAI of doing in its suit.
That filing names several former Apple employees and says they "surreptitiously accessed and downloaded dozens of Apple's confidential hardware-related files, including voluminous, detailed information about unreleased products, engineering presentations, technical specifications and proprietary project data."
In any event, the courts will have to settle this whole thing. We'll keep you posted as these two suits make their way through the legal system.

title: A New Breed of Chip Runs AI Models Using Waves of Light
text:
As artificial intelligence becomes an unavoidable part of everyday life and models become ever more sophisticated, the cost of the energy required to run the technology is ballooning.
To rein in runaway costs, AI labs and cloud providers are trying to build new data centers in places with cheap and plentiful renewable energy— like Scandinavia . But logistical challenges, a scarcity of key components , and a swell of anti-data center protests are getting in the way.
An expanding field of hardware startups, among them German company Q.ANT, is coming at the problem from a different direction: by developing a new breed of chip— photonic processors —meant to minimize the amount of energy that AI models consume.
Whereas regular GPUs transmit and process data by shuffling electrons around, photonic processors use waves of light. Because light doesn’t generate heat as it travels and allows more data to be processed simultaneously, photonic processors supposedly consume less energy and require minimal cooling—one of the largest sources of cost for data centers.
The aim isn’t to replace GPUs with photonic processors, but to run them side-by-side. Whilst GPUs excel at grinding through masses of additions and multiplications—linear math—photonic processors are best suited to complex, nonlinear calculations.
Few photonic processors are running inside data centers today. But Q.ANT recently rolled out its chips to facilities operated by cloud company IONOS as part of a pilot program. It says that more than 30 teams of engineers are now developing AI models optimized for photonic computing.
Earlier this month, WIRED spoke with Michael Förtsch, founder and CEO of Q.ANT. We discussed the energy bottlenecks constraining AI development, how photonic processors differ from regular chips, and the challenges Q.ANT faces in trying to popularize a new class of hardware.
This conversation has been edited for length and clarity.
WIRED: Michael, could you start by outlining the problem Q.ANT is aiming to solve? Why does the world need photonic processors to run AI models?
Michael Förtsch: The overall problem is the cost generated by the huge amount of energy consumption.
If you compute the way we think light should be used—not as a direct replacement for a GPU, but as a coprocessor—you basically have a new processor that takes care of the heavy math.
The cost driver today is the access to the memory. The less data you need in order to complete a job, the more efficient and better your system. We execute complicated math in a single step, where [regular chips] need thousands of steps. This saves a bunch of data—or memory access points.
How would you explain to the layperson how photonic computing works? How can light be used to perform mathematical computations?
Light is a wave. What is a wave? A sine function . [ The sine function is a mathematical rule that, when plotted to a graph, produces a smooth repeating wave. —Editor ] If I want to model something that’s round in shape with only linear functions, I need an infinite amount of data points and lines in order to describe something very simple: a circle. If I have the sine function at hand, because light is a wave, I need two points and I have already described the circle in all its beauty.
Light is very, very gifted to operate on complicated equations.
What distinguishes the type of problem best left to regular chips from problems that should be delegated to photonic processors?
The Nvidia H200 GPU is a masterpiece of technology. It’s art. It’s truly hard to attack it in its homeground. But light has strengths where the GPU is weak—and vice versa.
Linear math? Please route it to the GPU. Non-linear and complex stuff? Please route it to us.
We believe we will be much stronger in everything related to pictures and videos: image recognition, segmentation, and generation. Then, everything that’s related to robotics and physical AI.
What is the estimated gain in energy efficiency tied to using photonic processors alongside GPUs for AI tasks?
I’m not saying photonic computing will come for free. But I see that photonic computing, in combination with [CPUs and GPUs], can bring you a lot more artificial intelligence at a fraction of the energy.
Under simulation, we are ending up at around four or five times energy reduction. But in real hardware we are not yet demonstrating it.
Can any task run on photonic hardware by default, or do they need to be configured in a certain way?
There’s no need to learn a different language than C++ or Python. And you can already execute [preexisting] code on our machines.
But if you take something that has been optimized for a GPU only, you should not expect that automatically things will run faster. You have to do some adaptations.
It’s a chicken and egg problem, right? Until developers are building models to run on this type of processor, it’s going to be difficult to sell them to cloud providers. Equally, until photonic processors are available for people to use, it’s going to be tough to convince developers to design for them.
Whether it’s photonic or any other processor technology, it will need time to get the credibility and trust that’s needed for a company like Google to build data center infrastructure around it.
That’s the reason we chose to go into data centers with proof of concept systems, to validate that photonic computing is robust enough to withstand that environment.
We want to invite the world to compute on our systems. We are building a new chicken, so you can start producing eggs. Let’s find out together whether they’re tasty or not.
What else should I understand about why photonic processors are not already widely in use?
If hypothetically we received an order of 100,000 [photonic processors], we at Q.ANT are ready, but I’m not sure about the suppliers.
Hardware is not software. On the assembly side, it will need [time] before we have the same robust supply chain as the semiconductor world.
Do you expect to suffer from the same problem as other hardware challengers in securing capacity with the big chip manufacturers?
[To produce Q.ANT chips] you only need 90 nanometer node technology, from the 2000s. A lot of foundries already use this capability to produce chips that are super cheap. With this technology, you can use the same line to produce high-performance chips with a much higher street price, without massive upfront investment in your assets.
That resonates well with the industry.
Are Q.ANT processors built to function alongside a particular brand of GPUs—say, Nvidia or AMD—or are they totally agnostic?
There’s no need to go single-sided with a particular GPU. We want to have the freedom to cooperate with any of them.
Either way, we are not competitive to GPUs, we complete their function set.
Can you imagine a future in which AI models run entirely on photonic processors, or will they always be a sidekick?
If we see an opportunity in five years to attack the GPU as well, we would not be sh

title: LA school district blocks Google's AI search features
text:
LA school district blocks Google's AI search features
The company has insisted that AI overviews and search are a package deal.
After Google spent the past month telling schools that its search engine and AI were too "deeply integrated" to be separated , one of the biggest school districts in the country ripped them apart nonetheless. The AP reports that Los Angeles Unified School Distict (LAUSD), which enrolls about half a million students, quietly disabled Google's AI Overviews on school-issued devices.
Although LAUSD didn't make a formal announcement, parents and students noticed the missing AI summaries in search results. That prompted a local advocacy group, Schools Beyond Screens LA, to ask parents to send video evidence. The group then received confirmation from the school district that AI Overviews were indeed disabled, albeit without details on the exact method used. (Third-party tools seem a likely candidate.)
The move came after a Nov. 13 meeting of LAUSD's AI committee, where several Schools Beyond Screens members spoke. A few days later, the AI summaries had vanished from school devices. The district describes the change as temporary and about keeping students' experience "age-appropriate and safe."
Earlier this month, Google walked back one policy on AI in schools that had sparked a backlash: switching on its Gemini chatbot by default for many K-12 students. (Google's AI tools will now be opt-in for students.) But at the same time, the company insisted that the connection between search and AI was a different story. Google VP & General Manager of Education, Chris Phillips, told The New York Times that "search and AI are deeply integrated," and that if a district blocked AI, students "will not have access to Search, and they'll see a message from their school that indicates it's not available."
If that sounds like Google throwing its weight around to justify its massive AI spending , well, some of the company's own workers might agree. Over 500 of them signed a petition earlier this month , asking their employer to reconsider the strict requirements.
If Google doesn't back down, it could be risking a significant loss of business. New York City, Los Angeles and Chicago are all considering switching search engines if it comes to that.

title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
text:
Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine ( trn3.48xlarge , 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work.
With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos?
I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result.
Two goals
I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API.
For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines.
How it works
The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened:
Each shot has a name and a prompt , and can have a seed , to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next:
from : the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion.
to : the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it.
A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it.
Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames ( to ), and the shots after it start from its last frames ( from ). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg .
The payoff is iceberg : the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap , the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg ( to ), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg ( from ): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest.
On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5 . LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline , upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps.
The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. The film part is about 160 lines of Python on top: read the film file, order the shots so each keyframe exists before the shot that needs it, and cut the frames to hand over; then trim, caption, even out the sound and assemble the film. The code is in dacorvo/video-generation . The films I kept are in the dacorvo/video-generation bucket, with their JSON files: the seal, the fox, and the goat, which trims two of its shots and draws a caption over its payoff.
Running on Trainium3
Out of the box, the model does not run on the NeuronCores: the transformer does not fit on one, and diffusers has no plan to split it. The first attempt that ran (the model card's pipeline, with the transformer split over 4 cores and a few patches) took about 5 min 20 s for a 10-second clip, and the NeuronCores were actually computing for only about 45 s of it. What's more, the target resolution was out of reach.
First attempt, 960×544

Getting there took three kinds of work: making the model run on the NeuronCores (requires tensor parallelism), splitting it over more of them (sequence parallelism), and making the host keep up with them.
Most of the fixes below are on the device, and that is where most of the effort went. The biggest end-to-end savings came from the host: the low-hanging fruit, since that is obviously where the waste was.
What it took to make it work
The transformer does not fit on one NeuronCore, and diffusers has no tensor-parallel plan for it
A plan , and an attention processor that runs on the heads of one rank
The transformer runs on 4 cores
The text encoder does not fit on a NeuronCore next to the transformer, so it runs on the CPUs. diffusers supports a pipeline split this way, but its LTX-2 pipelines give the text encoder its inputs on the NeuronCores
Pin the pipeline to the host, and move the transformer's inputs to the cores and its outputs back
The pipeline runs with its transformer on the cores
Compiled as one graph, the transformer returned NaN at one size, and each new process traced it again, even with every graph in the cache
Compile one block with compile_repeated_blocks
Finite outputs, and tracing falls from 388 s to 18 s
torch-neuronx computes a bf16 GELU entirely in bf16, constants included ( #1049 )
Compute the GELUs in fp32
Transformer error against fp32: 0.297 → 0.158 (CPU bf16: 0.160)
At 2048×1024, the block graph of the transformer split 4 ways fails to load
Split the video tokens 8 ways on top (sequence parallelism): two custom attention processors on diffusers' set_attn_processor hook, each a few tensor reshapes around its collective calls ( code )
Stage 2 runs on 4 × 8 = 32 cores, at 3.0 s a step
A shot that starts from frames has a timestep per video token, and its block graph fails to load
Embed only the two timesteps, and pick one for each token ( code )
A shot from frames takes about as long as one from a prompt
What it took to make it fast
Each rank (one process per NeuronCore) ran the whole pipeline, and they all encoded the prompt on the CPUs of one socket

title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
text:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
Title: How Much Effort Does an AI Code Reviewer Need? Evidence from Claude 5.5 Models on Plausible-but-Wrong Patches
Abstract: AI coding agents write code faster than people can review it, so teams add AI reviewers. Reasoning models let such a reviewer trade cost for diligence through an effort setting. We asked how much effort a reviewer needs to catch plausible-but-wrong patches, which pass a benchmark's tests but fail stronger ones. Claude Opus 5.5 (preregistered), Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (exploratory) each reviewed the same 90 agent-written Django patches from SWE-bench Verified at low, medium and high effort. By strengthened SWE-ABS tests, 55 patches were wrong and 35 correct. In every model, high effort accepted fewer wrong patches than low (false success .45 against .67 for Opus, .49 against .65 for Sonnet, .51 against .78 for Haiku), a supported difference for Opus and Haiku. For Opus, medium was non-inferior to high within 15 percentage points (difference .018, 95% CI [-.065, .108]) and cost 20% less, short of the preregistered 30%. For Sonnet and Haiku, medium cost 39% and 51% less than high but was not shown non-inferior. Opus at medium or high agreed best with the labels; Haiku at high cost about 8% as much per review as Opus at medium, accuracy difference unresolved. Exploratory coding showed that most rejections named the tested defect and that effort added such rejections. No setting is a strong gate: each accepted at least 45% of wrong patches. For 32 of the 55 wrong patches the issue may not require what the failing test checks; without them, neither accuracy hypothesis holds for any model.
